properties.decision:
Recorded as BRAINSTORMING, not as a proposal. Anthony, 2026-09-06, in his words: 'we had brainstormed removing rocksdb before and going with the in-memory as the only option. would redis-rs be an option or fred (another rust crate for redis)? would they interface with kv_backend trait? would there be any benefit of going with redis versus rocksdb or with strictly in-memory option?'

WHAT THE SEAM IS (read from backend.rs): `KvBackend` is six SYNCHRONOUS functions — get, put, delete, prefix_scan, prefix_delete, commit_batch(ops) — over named column families, with ONE stated performance contract: prefix iteration must be ORDERED (the memory backend moved HashMap -> BTreeMap for it, chg:the-memory-backend-keeps-its-keys-ordered; the network build's determinism rests on (from,type,to) key order). Two impls today: MemoryBackend and RocksBackend.

WOULD REDIS FIT IT? Yes, with three adaptations, none free. (1) ORDERING: Redis has no ordered keyspace — SCAN MATCH is unordered and O(whole keyspace). An ordered prefix_scan needs each column family modelled as a sorted set of keys (ZADD at score 0; ZRANGEBYLEX [prefix [prefix\\xff) plus a value store per key — two round trips or one Lua script per scan. (2) ATOMICITY: commit_batch maps to MULTI/EXEC (or a Lua script); reads inside the batch see the pre-batch state, which is what the engine's write buffer already assumes. (3) SYNC-OVER-ASYNC: the seam is sync and is called under the async server's write lock; redis-rs has a sync connection API and fits directly but blocks a tokio worker per call (needs spawn_blocking or a dedicated thread); fred is async-only and would need block_on inside a sync trait — awkward — or the seam made async, which touches every caller. redis-rs is the more natural fit for the seam as it stands.

THE OPTIONS:
(a) ROCKSDB, status quo — embedded, ordered, durable; costs a C++ build (req:platform already says consumers must not pay it for a routine update; dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds is open on exactly this).
(b) IN-MEMORY ONLY, export document as the truth — the earlier brainstorm (dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability; dec:idea-the-store-becomes-a-session-cache-and-the-export-becomes-the-truth). Measured: 1,452 core tests pass with no store; hydrate is 0.91 s at 3,140 nodes after the write-buffer fix (was 8.8 s), but fact:hydrating-from-the-document-costs-16x-a-store-open says a store still buys startup.
(c) REDIS via redis-rs — network KV; ordered-set encoding for scans; MULTI for batches; sync client.
(d) REDIS via fred — async-first, pooling, cluster, reconnection; needs the seam made async or a runtime bridge.
properties.name: OPEN — would Redis (via redis-rs or fred) be a third backend option behind the KvBackend seam, and would it buy anything over RocksDB or an in-memory-only store with the export as the truth?
properties.rationale: WHAT REDIS WOULD BUY, honestly separated from what it would not. IT WOULD BUY: (1) one LIVE graph shared across processes AND machines — the thing neither an embedded store nor in-memory can do, and the only benefit here that is distinctive; today many-people-on-one-design holds through ONE shared server process (cap:shared-sessions) and git-transported exports, and the fact that 'the design graph does not branch with git' bit this very session four times. (2) Push instead of poll for 'the record moved' via pub/sub. (3) No C++ build (the compiles-in-seconds problem dissolves — for consumers who can run a daemon). (4) Durability for free via RDB/AOF. IT WOULD NOT BUY, and would cost: (1) LATENCY ON THE READ LOOP — the detectors make thousands of point reads per rollup (node_types_holding alone is 29 per resolution; all_defects was measured at 3.45 s of mostly compute over in-process reads). A local Redis round trip is ~50-100 µs on a unix socket, ~200 µs on TCP, against ~100 ns in-process: fifty thousand reads per rollup becomes +5-10 s, and the detectors are sequential so pipelining helps little. The loop's whole 2026-09-05 optimisation would be undone by the transport. (2) AN EXTERNAL DAEMON IN THE INSTALL STORY — 'one-liner install, one-word update' (user-iterative-release-preference) becomes 'and run Redis'; Alex's Grok Build TUI environment and the kit consumers would all need it. (3) A security and identity surface — design content over a socket, auth, one Redis holding many graphs (the key layout already prefixes by graph_id, so that half exists). (4) The ordering contract met by construction in BTreeMap and RocksDB becomes an encoding discipline in Redis that every scan must honour. A RANKING, AS A FINDING NOT A DECISION: Redis answers a DIFFERENT question from the one the byte-store brainstorms asked. They asked 'what does an embedded store buy over the document'; Redis asks 'does the live graph need to be shared across processes and machines'. If the answer to the second is NO (the shared server suffices), Redis is an external dependency and a latency tax for nothing, and (b)-with-optional-embedded-store remains the cheaper road. If the answer is YES — Alex's team on one live design, the storyflow fleet — then a network KV behind the SAME seam is the natural shape, redis-rs fits the sync seam today, and the read-loop latency becomes the constraint to design around (caching the detector reads per write generation, which DerivedMemo already begins). NOT MEASURED: any Redis number here — the latencies are typical figures, not reflow2's; a spike behind the seam on a copy of the live store would take a day and answer this properly. Anthony rules; nothing is built.
